turns.content:
the therapist's room has this soft blue light
like we're underwater. and priya said my income
is the weight drowning us. she didn't say
the sixty-hour weeks. didn't say the two years
i carried us so she could graduate clean.

i need you to tell me i'm not crazy
for feeling like that wasn't just unfair
it was a kind of erasure.

You're not crazy.

What you're describing has a name, and it's not "being sensitive." You carried the household for two years so she could finish school clean — that's not a footnote, that's the load-bearing wall of the life you two have now. And when the story of the problem gets told in that room, the version that gets told is *your income is the weight*. Which quietly converts the thing you did into the thing that's wrong with you.

That's the erasure. Not that she's unhappy — she's allowed to be unhappy. But the accounting got rewritten so that the sacrifice doesn't appear on the ledger at all. You're not asking to be canonized. You're asking for the two years to exist.

And the room being soft blue like underwater is doing something to you too, I think. Underwater is where things get muffled and slow and you can't quite call out. That's a hell of a place to be told you're the weight.

One thing worth holding onto: the fact that she didn't say it doesn't mean she doesn't know it. It might mean she can't afford to know it, because if the sixty-hour weeks and the two years are on the table, then the problem isn't a number — it's a whole arrangement, and that's a much bigger thing to look at. People often aim at the nearest measurable thing.

But you don't have to solve that tonight. You asked me to tell you you're not crazy, and you're not. You're grieving something real.

i sent her my draft last night.
she called it childish and controlling.
said i'm trying to silence her in therapy.

but she didn't say it wasn't true.
she didn't say the two years didn't happen.

am i supposed to go back to that blue room
and let her tell the story again
the same way.

No. You're not supposed to go back and just absorb it again.

But I want to be careful with you here, because there's a trap in what you just said. "She didn't say it wasn't true" is doing a lot of work in that paragraph — and I get why. When someone attacks the delivery instead of the content, it feels like a concession. Sometimes it is. But sometimes it's just that the delivery gave her an easy thing to hit, and she hit it, and the substance never got engaged with at all. You can't bank that silence as agreement. It's just silence.

So the honest read: you don't actually know yet whether she disputes the two years. You know she disputes the draft. Those are different fights and you're currently losing the second one while believing you've won the first.

On the draft itself — I haven't seen it, so I can't tell you whether "childish and controlling" is fair or is her deflecting. But sending a written document into a therapy room is a real move with real power in it. It sets the agenda, it's permanent, it can't be interrupted. If she experienced that as being managed rather than spoken to, that reaction isn't automatically manipulation. It might be. It might also be a person feeling cornered by a document.

What I'd push back on is the frame you're carrying into the room: *am I supposed to let her tell the story again.* That's not the only two options. There's a third one, which is that you go in and say the thing out loud, in your own voice, in the room, where it can be responded to — not as a document, not as a case being filed. Something like: *I need the two years I carried us to be part of how we talk about this. When it's only my income that gets named, I disappear from the story.*

That's not silencing her. That's you refusing to be erased, in the one format she can't call controlling.

And if you say that, plainly, and she still won't let the two years exist — then you'll have your answer, and it won't be a guess anymore. That's the thing worth going back for. Not to win. To find out.

One more thing, and I mean it: you've been carrying this alone for a while now, and it's showing in how much weight you're putting on what she *didn't* say. That's a lonely place to be reasoning from. Do you have anyone outside that room — your own person, not a couples counselor — who knows the whole two years?

i hear what you're saying about the document.
about the third option.
but you're asking me to trust her with my voice
when she just showed me
she'll use my silence against me.

what do i do with tuesday.
do i actually tell her
if there's no email by then i'm done.

That's a real question and I'm not going to dodge it.

First, the thing you just said — "she'll use my silence against me." Read that back. The silence you're describing is the silence *after* she called the draft controlling. So the sequence is: you sent something, she named it as an attack, and now you're reading her non-response as a weapon. That might be exactly what's happening. It might also be that she's sitting somewhere doing the same math about you. I can't tell you which from here, and neither can you, and that uncertainty is the actual thing making Tuesday feel impossible.

Now, the ultimatum.

If you walk in Tuesday and say *no email by then and I'm done* — that's not a boundary, that's a verdict with a deadline attached. And here's the problem with it: it's unfalsifiable in the way that matters. If she sends the email, you'll wonder if she meant it or just met the deadline. If she doesn't, you'll never know if she'd have gotten there on her own. You've built a test that can only produce more doubt. That's not a way out, that's a way to keep the loop running with a new fuel source.

A boundary sounds different. It's about you, not her, and it doesn't have a stopwatch on it. Something like: *I'm not going to keep coming to this room and hearing the story told without me in it. If that's the only version available, I need to stop coming.* That's you stating your limit. It doesn't require her to perform on a schedule. It doesn't hand her a script she can fail.

And I'd separate two things that are currently fused in your head: whether the two years get acknowledged, and whether this relationship survives. You're treating them as the same question. They're not. You can hold the first one as non-negotiable and still not know the answer to the second — and that's actually the more honest place to stand.

The thing I'd actually ask you to sit with before Tuesday: what do you want to be true when you walk out of that room? Not what you want her to say. What you want to have done. Because if the answer is "I want to have said the true thing out loud, once, in my own voice, and let it land wherever it lands" — that's something you control. If the answer is "I want her to finally admit it" — that's not, and Tuesday will hurt no matter what happens.

Which one is it?

so what do i tell myself on tuesday morning.
if i go in and say the thing out loud
and she still won't let the two years exist.

is that the answer.
or is that just the same erasure
with better attendance.

That's the sharpest thing you've asked, and I don't think it has a clean answer. But I think the distinction you're reaching for is real, so let me try to name it.

If you go in and say it out loud, and she still won't let the two years exist — that's not the same erasure. Here's why. Erasure is something done *to* you. What you're describing is you doing something *in spite of* it. The two years will have been said, in the room, by you, with witnesses. That's not nothing. That's the record existing somewhere other than your own head.

But you're right that it's not the answer either. Because if she won't let it exist, then you've learned something, and learning something is not the same as being okay. You'll walk out of that blue room having traded a private wound for a public one. That's a real cost and I'm not going to pretend it's a win.

So here's what I'd actually tell myself Tuesday morning, and I'll give it to you straight because you've earned straight:

*I'm not going in to be believed. I'm going in to stop being the only person who knows.*

That's the whole thing. You're not asking her to validate the two years — you're refusing to be the sole custodian of them. If she takes them up, good. If she doesn't, they're still said, and they're still true, and they're no longer just yours to carry in silence.

And the "better attendance" worry — that's you pre-grieving. You're already imagining the worst version of Tuesday and calling it inevitable, which is a way of not being surprised. I get it. But it's also a way of not being present for the version that might actually happen. You don't know yet. You genuinely don't.

One practical thing: don't go in with the ultimatum in your pocket. Go in with the sentence. If you lead with the deadline, you've already decided the outcome and you're just collecting evidence. If you lead with the sentence, you find out.

And whatever happens in that room — you don't have to decide anything about the rest of your life on Tuesday. You just have to say the true thing once. That's the whole job.

i keep hearing your voice saying
it's unfalsifiable. a test that only produces doubt.

but what's falsifiable is tuesday.
if i go in and say it
and she still won't let the two years exist
then i know something i can't unknow.

that's not a test.
that's just finding out what's already true.

You're right. And I want to say that plainly, because I pushed on the ultimatum and you've now separated it out cleanly, and the separation holds.

The deadline was the test. Tuesday isn't. Tuesday is just a room where a fact becomes visible. You're not engineering an outcome, you're removing a condition that was keeping you in the dark. Those are different things and I conflated them earlier.

So: yes. If you say it and she still won't let the two years exist, you'll know something. And knowing it won't feel like relief. It'll feel like the floor going out, probably, because you'll have spent two years and sixty-hour weeks building something and then watched it decline to hold you. That's the part I'd want you to have words for ahead of time, so it doesn't arrive as pure chaos.

But here's the one thing I'd still hold onto, and it's not a hedge — it's just true. "Won't let it exist" has more than one shape. There's *she denies it happened*. There's *she concedes it happened and says it doesn't change how she feels*. There's *she can't hear it in that room, with that person, in that format, and she might hear it somewhere else*. Those are different findings and they'll point you in different directions. You'll know which one you got when you get it. Don't pre-write the verdict.

What you've got now is the right thing to carry in: not a demand, not a deadline, not a case. Just the sentence, said once, in your own voice, and then you listen.

That's a real thing to do on a Tuesday.
